title: Samuel Steps Aside
sum: With Saul now king, Samuel stands before all Israel at Gilgal and asks them to testify: has he ever taken an ox, a donkey or a bribe? They clear him. Then he puts the people on trial. He reviews their history, from Egypt through the judges, as a story of the LORD rescuing them each time they cried out. Yet when Nahash attacked, they demanded a king, though the LORD was their king.

To show the weight of their choice, Samuel calls on the LORD, and thunder and rain fall during the wheat harvest, the dry season. The terrified people beg him to pray for them. Samuel answers with grace: the LORD will not abandon his people, for his own name's sake. Samuel will never stop praying for them. Only fear the LORD and serve him, or king and people alike will be swept away.
readings: Read as a farewell speech

Like Moses (Deuteronomy 31–33) and Joshua (Joshua 23–24), Samuel marks the end of an era with a speech that reviews history and lays out the choice ahead. Scholars see these speeches as pillars of the history that runs from Deuteronomy to Kings. The era of the judges is over; the era of the kings begins, under the same covenant.
Read as a trial

The language is the law court: "testify against me," "witness," "I will take you to court." First Samuel is acquitted, then Israel is found guilty. The thunder is God's verdict. But the sentence is mercy: the covenant still stands if the people and their king obey.

views.H: Samuel gave this address at Gilgal soon after Saul's victory over Nahash, early in Saul's reign (traditionally dated about 1030–1010 BC, all dates approximate). The thunderstorm in the dry season was a real sign that confirmed his words.
views.C: Critical scholars assign the speech to the Deuteronomistic editors, who placed such speeches at the turning points of their history. It belongs to the strand that sees the monarchy as a rejection of God, though it allows a king under the covenant.
views.L: Literary readers notice Samuel's self-defense: he insists on his honesty while the whole chapter shows how hard he finds it to give up power. He is now the prophet beside the king, a pattern for the rest of the books of Kings.
views.J: The rabbis compared Samuel to Moses and Aaron (Psalm 99:6), and read 12:3 as a model of a leader who takes nothing from the people. The phrase "his great name" became a basis for trusting God's faithfulness despite Israel's sin.
views.X: Christian readers see in Samuel's "I will never sin ... by giving up praying for you" a model of intercessory ministry, and in God's choice not to abandon his people a theme Paul develops in Romans 11:1–2.

deep.b: Wheat harvest in Israel falls in May and June, after the winter rains have ended. Rain at that time is rare, and the Proverbs use it as a picture of something out of place (Proverbs 26:1). A sudden storm could ruin the grain lying in the fields. So the sign is a warning that cuts both ways: the LORD who sends the rain can also withhold it or send it to destroy. The God who sent thunder against Egypt (Exodus 9:23) and on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:16) and who thundered against the Philistines at Mizpah (7:10) now thunders against his own people's request.

Samuel's list of judges (12:11) has puzzled readers since antiquity. The Hebrew names Jerubbaal (Gideon), Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel. No judge called Bedan is known. The Greek and Syriac read Barak, which fits the order of Judges. The rabbis took Bedan as Samson, "the son of Dan." The Plain follows Barak and keeps Samuel. See the textual notes.

echoes: Deuteronomy 31–33; Joshua 23–24; 1 Kings 8:14–61; Psalm 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1; Romans 11:1–2; Hebrews 11:32

settings.to: all Israel, gathered at Gilgal with the new king Saul
settings.when: after Saul's victory, when the kingship is renewed at Gilgal
settings.why: Samuel steps aside as Israel's leader. First he asks the people to testify that he never took an ox or a bribe, which sets a standard for the king. Then he puts Israel on trial before the LORD, retelling how God rescued them from Egypt and in the days of the judges, though they kept forgetting him. He calls down thunder and rain at wheat harvest as a sign that asking for a king was evil. Yet he ends with hope: the LORD will not abandon his people for his name's sake, and Samuel will keep praying for them. Everything depends on whether king and people obey: "But if you keep doing evil, you and your king alike will be swept away" (12:25).
views: Traditional readers take it as Samuel's address at the renewal of the kingdom, a covenant ceremony like Joshua's at Shechem (Joshua 24).
A speech by the Deuteronomistic historian

Martin Noth counted it among the key speeches by which the historian marks turning points (with Joshua 23 and 1 Kings 8). On this view its last line speaks straight to the exiles, for whom king and people had indeed been swept away.

title: Saul Does Not Wait
sum: Saul's reign begins with a broken verse: his age and the length of his reign have dropped out of the Hebrew text. Jonathan strikes a Philistine post, and the Philistines answer with a huge army at Michmash. Israel's men hide in caves and cisterns or flee across the Jordan. Saul waits at Gilgal seven days for Samuel, as he was told (10:8), but as his troops drift away he offers the burnt offering himself.

Samuel arrives just as he finishes. Saul's kingdom will not last; the LORD has sought "a man to suit his own heart." The chapter ends with Israel almost unarmed: the Philistines have kept Israel from having smiths, so only Saul and Jonathan have swords.
readings: Read as a test failed

Samuel had told Saul to wait seven days (10:8). Saul waited, almost. His sin was not the sacrifice itself, since kings later offer sacrifices, but his refusal to wait for God's word through the prophet. The king must obey the LORD, not act on fear.
Read as a tragedy

Saul's reasons are understandable: the army is melting away, the enemy is near, and Samuel is late. Many readers find Samuel's verdict harsh. The narrator gives Saul's own words and lets the reader weigh them.

views.H: These events took place early in Saul's reign (the length of his reign is lost from 13:1). The Philistines' control of the smiths reflects a real policy of keeping the hill people dependent and disarmed.
views.C: Critical scholars often see 13:7b–15a as a later insertion that gives a first rejection of Saul, parallel to chapter 15. Without it, the story flows from Gilgal to the battle at Michmash.
views.L: The narrator builds tension with time: seven days, the time set, "just as he finished." Saul's long excuse (13:11–12) contrasts with Samuel's short verdict.
views.J: The rabbis read 13:1 as "Saul was as innocent as a year-old child" when he began to reign. The Talmud contrasts Saul, who sinned once (over Agag) and lost the kingdom, with David, who sinned twice and kept it (Yoma 22b).
views.X: "A man after his own heart" is quoted by Paul in his sermon at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:22), linked with Psalm 89:20 and Isaiah 44:28, as the description of David and the line that leads to Jesus.

deep.b: The verse literally says Saul was "a year old" when he became king and reigned "two years." Neither makes sense: Jonathan is already a commander. This is the standard formula for a king's reign (2 Samuel 5:4; 1 Kings 14:21), and both numbers seem to have fallen out of the text very early. Some Greek manuscripts fill in "thirty." Acts 13:21 gives Saul forty years. The Plain marks the gaps. See the textual note.

The Philistines kept Israel from making weapons by controlling the smiths (13:19–22). Israelites had to go to them to sharpen farm tools and paid a "pim," a weight about two-thirds of a shekel. Stone weights marked pym were found by archaeologists in the early 1900s, and they settled the meaning of a word that had puzzled translators for two thousand years (the KJV guessed "a file"). Older scholars spoke of a Philistine monopoly on iron, but the verse does not mention iron, and iron came into common use slowly across the whole region. Most historians now read it as political control: the Philistines kept Israel without smiths. Either way, Israel went to war almost unarmed, and its victories would have to come from the LORD.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two waits
deep.b: Saul's failure at Gilgal is a failure to wait. In the next chapter, Saul again cannot wait: he stops the priest mid-inquiry ("Pull your hand back," 14:19). By contrast David, in his long years on the run, repeatedly waits for God's time and refuses to seize the throne (24:6; 26:10–11). The book may be arranging its two kings around this one trait: the readiness to wait for the LORD.

settings.to: King Saul, at Gilgal
settings.when: just after Saul offers the burnt offering himself instead of waiting for Samuel, with the Philistines massing and his troops drifting away
settings.why: Samuel tells Saul he has acted like a fool and not kept the LORD's command, so his kingship will not last. The LORD has found "a man to suit his own heart." The fault seems small, but the point is that Israel's king must wait on God's word through the prophet. Readers already know who the new man will be. Paul quotes the line about David in Acts 13:22.
views: Some readers think the sin was offering sacrifice as a non-priest. Others note that kings did offer sacrifice (2 Samuel 6:17), and think the sin was not waiting the full time for Samuel, that is, not obeying the prophet's word.

title: Jonathan Climbs the Cliff
sum: While Saul sits under a pomegranate tree, Jonathan and his armor-bearer climb a cliff between two crags to attack a Philistine post. "The LORD is not held back," Jonathan says. "He can save with many or with few." They kill twenty men, the earth quakes, and panic sweeps the Philistine army. Israel joins the rout.

But Saul has forced an oath on the army: no food until evening. Jonathan, who did not hear it, tastes some honey. The hungry soldiers later eat meat with the blood. When God does not answer Saul's question, he casts lots, and the lot falls on Jonathan. Saul is ready to kill his son, but the people ransom him. The chapter ends with a summary of Saul's wars and family.
readings: Read as a hero story

Jonathan is the true hero: brave, trusting God, generous. His faith echoes Gideon's three hundred and anticipates David against Goliath. The victory is a "trembling from God," not a human achievement.
Read as a portrait of Saul

Every move Saul makes goes wrong: he waits too long, then rushes; he calls the priest, then stops him; he swears an oath that weakens his army and nearly kills his son. The people have to save Jonathan from their king.

views.H: The cliffs of Bozez and Seneh can be identified in the Wadi Suweinit between Geba and Michmash. In his 1923 memoir, the British officer Vivian Gilbert says a brigade major used this chapter in 1918 to find a path for a surprise attack on the Turkish position at Michmash; the story is not confirmed in the official histories.
views.C: Critical scholars see an old heroic tale about Jonathan, combined with stories about Saul's oath and an altar. The summary at the end (14:47–52) reads like a closing formula for Saul's reign, as if from an older account.
views.L: The chapter sets father and son side by side. Jonathan acts and trusts; Saul talks and swears. Jonathan's "My father has stirred up trouble for the land" (14:29) uses the word for Achan's sin (Joshua 7:25).
views.J: The rabbis praised Jonathan's faith and humility. They also used the people's ransom of Jonathan as an example of a vow that was annulled because it was wrongly made.
views.X: Christian readers see Jonathan's "save with many or with few" as a lesson in faith that does not count numbers. Some see his near-death under his father's oath, and his rescue, as a faint picture of the Son condemned under the law but delivered.

deep.b: Verse 41 is the only place in the Bible that shows how the Urim and Thummim may have worked, but only in the longer Greek and Latin text. There Saul prays: if the guilt is in me or Jonathan, give Urim; if it is in the people, give Thummim. The Hebrew has just two words, "Give perfect," probably because a scribe's eye skipped. The Plain follows the longer reading, as most modern translations do. The procedure answered yes-or-no questions, narrowing down from groups to individuals, as with Achan (Joshua 7:14–18).

The starving soldiers slaughtered animals "on the ground" and ate them with the blood (14:32). The law forbade eating blood (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10–14; Deuteronomy 12:16). Saul has a large stone brought so animals can be killed properly and the blood drained. This is his first altar to the LORD (14:35). The scene shows Saul caring about the law even while his own oath caused the sin.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the king's oath and the judge's vow
deep.b: Saul's oath recalls Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:30–40): a leader's rash words before battle put his own child under a death sentence. Jephthah kept his vow; Saul is stopped by the people. The book may be showing that the new kingship, unlike the time of the judges, has a check on it: the people themselves can say "Far from it!" to a king.

settings.to: his armor-bearer, at the pass of Michmash
settings.when: while Saul sits under a pomegranate tree with six hundred men
settings.why: Jonathan says the LORD can save "with many or with few," and sets a sign: if the Philistines call them up, God has handed them over. His words show the kind of trust Saul lacks. They also prepare the way for David's words to Goliath (17:47).

settings.to: his troops, the men of Israel, on the day of battle
settings.when: while they chase the Philistines
settings.why: Saul puts a curse on anyone who eats before evening, "until I take revenge on my enemies." An oath like this bound the whole army before God. It was meant to win God's favor, but it weakened the troops, led them to eat meat with the blood, and nearly cost Jonathan his life. The narrator shows a king whose religious zeal serves himself.

settings.what: Saul's order on eating meat with the blood
settings.to: his starving troops, after the battle near Aijalon
settings.when: when the people slaughter captured animals on the ground and eat them with the blood
settings.why: Saul has a large stone rolled up and orders every man to slaughter his animal there, so the blood can drain away. The law forbade eating blood, because the life is in the blood (Leviticus 17:10–14; Deuteronomy 12:16, 23–24). The order binds every soldier in the field, far from a sanctuary. It shows Saul's concern for the law, though the trouble came from his own oath.

settings.what: Saul's oath against Jonathan, and the people's answer
settings.to: the leaders and the whole army, before the LORD
settings.when: when God gives no answer about attacking that night
settings.why: Saul swears that the guilty one must die, even if it is his son. The lot falls on Jonathan. But the people swear back, by the life of the LORD, that Jonathan will not lose a hair, because he worked with God that day. The people's oath overrules the king's. Readers see Saul's hold on his people, and on God's favor, slipping.

title: Listening Is Better Than Sacrifice
sum: Samuel orders Saul to put Amalek under the ban, destroying people and animals, because of what Amalek did to Israel on the road from Egypt. Saul wins the battle but spares King Agag and the best animals. The LORD tells Samuel, "I regret making Saul king." Samuel cries out all night.

Saul greets Samuel with a claim of obedience, but the sheep are bleating. He blames the people and says the animals are for sacrifice. Samuel answers in poetry: listening is better than sacrifice. Saul confesses, but too late. As Samuel turns away, Saul grabs his robe and it tears: the kingdom is torn from him. Samuel himself kills Agag, and he and Saul never meet again.
readings: Read as obedience and sacrifice

The heart of the chapter is Samuel's poem (15:22–23). Worship without obedience is empty. The prophets will repeat it: Hosea 6:6, Micah 6:6–8, Psalm 51:16–17. Saul's offering of the spoil was religion used as an excuse.
Read as a hard text

Modern readers are troubled by the command to kill women and children, and so were ancient ones: the Talmud has Saul himself protest that the children and animals had done nothing (Yoma 22b), and Maimonides rules that peace must be offered first even to Amalek. Some scholars (Copan and Flannagan, following Younger) read the language as ancient war hyperbole; others (Seibert) say it reflects Israel's understanding at the time, which later revelation corrects; traditional readers see a unique judgment. See the topic on holy war.

views.H: Saul's campaign against Amalek took place in the Negev and Sinai, some years into his reign. God's command was a judgment on Amalek for its long hostility (Exodus 17:8–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19).
views.C: Most critical scholars see this as a prophetic story that explains why Saul's dynasty failed, from the circles that valued prophets above kings. It doubles the rejection of chapter 13.
views.L: Literary readers follow the word "listen" (shama'), which runs through the chapter, and the word "regret" (nacham), used of God in 15:11 and 15:35 but denied in 15:29. The tearing robe is one of the book's great images.
views.J: Jewish tradition connects Agag to Haman "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1). Because Saul spared Agag, the line survived to threaten the Jews in Persia. This chapter is read as the haftarah for Shabbat Zakhor, before Purim.
views.X: Christian readers see Saul's sin as partial obedience, and Samuel's poem as a call to worship from the heart (Romans 12:1). The church fathers wrestled with 15:29 and 15:11 as a test case for how Scripture speaks of God's changelessness.

deep.b: Twice the chapter says the LORD regretted making Saul king (15:11; 15:35), and between them Samuel says "Israel's Enduring One does not lie and does not regret. He is not a human being, to have regrets" (15:29). Interpreters have read this tension in several ways. Classical theology (Augustine, Calvin, Maimonides) holds that God does not change, and that "regret" describes God's actions in human terms. Others read the verses as saying God's grief is real but his decision about Saul is final. Some modern theologians (open theists) take the regret more literally. See the topic on God's regret.

Haman is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), and Mordecai is a Benjaminite descended from Kish (Esther 2:5). The rabbis read the book of Esther as the sequel to this chapter: Saul's descendant Mordecai finishes the war Saul failed to complete, against Agag's descendant Haman. On the Sabbath before Purim, Jews read Deuteronomy 25:17–19 (remember Amalek) and this chapter.

echoes: Exodus 17:8–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8; Psalm 51:16–17; Esther 3:1; Numbers 23:19; 1 Kings 11:29–31

settings.what: The command to put Amalek under the ban
settings.by: Samuel, speaking for the LORD of Armies
settings.to: King Saul
settings.when: during Saul's reign; the text gives no date
settings.why: God orders Saul to strike Amalek and destroy everything, people and animals, as punishment for Amalek's attack on Israel on the way out of Egypt (Exodus 17:8–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19). The command is a test of whether Saul will obey God's word fully. The rest of the chapter turns on his partial obedience.
views: Holy war in its ancient setting

Many readers explain the ban (herem) as an ancient practice of giving all spoil to the deity, known also from the Moabite Mesha Stele. They read the story as being about obedience, not a model for any later war.

Many Jewish and Christian readers have struggled with a command to kill children. The rabbis took up Saul's argument for mercy and rejected it (Bavli Yoma 22b, citing Ecclesiastes 7:16: do not be overly righteous). Later Jewish law limited how such a command could ever be applied: peace must be offered first (Maimonides, Laws of Kings 6). Many modern readers see the command as reflecting Israel's beliefs about war, not God's lasting will.

settings.to: King Saul, at Gilgal
settings.when: after Saul spares Agag and the best animals and claims he obeyed
settings.why: Samuel answers Saul's excuse that the animals were for sacrifice with a short poem: the LORD wants listening more than burnt offerings, and rebellion is as bad as fortune-telling. Because Saul rejected the LORD's word, the LORD has rejected him as king. The prophets later made the same point (Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24; Micah 6:6–8). For Israel's readers, it put obedience above ritual.

settings.to: King Saul, as Samuel turns to leave Gilgal
settings.when: when Saul confesses but begs Samuel to come back with him
settings.why: As Samuel turns, "he caught" the robe and it ripped. The Hebrew does not say who caught whose robe; the Dead Sea scroll and the Greek say Saul. When the robe rips, Samuel turns the accident into a sign: the LORD has torn the kingdom from Saul and given it to a neighbor who is better than he. Israel's God "does not lie and does not regret." The words make the rejection final and point ahead to David. Readers later saw Ahijah tear a robe in the same way (1 Kings 11:30–31).

settings.to: Agag king of Amalek, before the LORD at Gilgal
settings.when: just before Samuel kills him
settings.why: Samuel's two-line verdict says Agag's sword left mothers childless, so his own mother will be childless. It presents his death as justice for his own crimes, not only as the ban. Samuel does what Saul would not.

title: The LORD Sees the Heart
sum: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem, under cover of a sacrifice, to anoint one of Jesse's sons. Samuel is impressed by the tall eldest son, Eliab, but the LORD says: "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart." Seven sons pass by. The youngest, out with the sheep, is called in, and the LORD says, "He is the one." From that day the LORD's Spirit sweeps down on David.

At the same moment, the Spirit leaves Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD terrifies him. His servants look for a musician, and one recommends a son of Jesse. So David comes to court, and his playing brings Saul relief. Saul loves him and makes him his armor-bearer.
readings: Read as election

God chooses the youngest, the one not even invited. The pattern runs through Genesis (Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim) and through the judges (Gideon). It means God's choice is not based on human standards.
Read as a story of two Spirits

The chapter is built on one exchange: the Spirit comes on David (16:13) and leaves Saul (16:14). David's music then soothes the spirit that troubles Saul. The new king serves the old one, even as he replaces him.

views.H: David was anointed privately as a youth, during Saul's reign (traditionally about 1030–1010 BC). He was later anointed publicly by Judah (2 Samuel 2:4) and by all Israel (2 Samuel 5:3).
views.C: Most critical scholars see 16:1–13 as a later prophetic story that places David's choice before his rise, and 16:14–23 as the start of the older "History of David's Rise."
views.L: Readers note the irony: the LORD warns against looks, and then David is described as handsome. The narrator keeps David silent throughout; he does not speak until chapter 17.
views.J: The rabbis said that Jesse's sons passed before Samuel and he expected to anoint each one. They also taught that the oil bubbled up of its own accord when David came near. Jesse's lineage from Ruth (Ruth 4:17–22) is an important part of Jewish tradition about David.
views.X: The church has read this chapter as a type of Christ: the anointed (Messiah) shepherd from Bethlehem, chosen by God, filled with the Spirit (Isaiah 11:1–2; Luke 2:4–11).

deep.h: An evil spirit from the LORD
deep.b: How can a spirit from the LORD be evil? The Hebrew ra'ah means "harmful" or "bad" as well as morally evil. The Targum keeps the phrase: "an evil spirit from before the LORD." Readers have taken it in several ways: a demon permitted by God (Josephus); a punishment sent by God, like the spirit sent between Abimelech and Shechem (Judges 9:23) or the lying spirit of 1 Kings 22:19–23; or an illness of the mind. That last view is old: the medieval Jewish commentators Radak and Ralbag explained Saul's spirit as melancholy. Critical scholars note that early Israel traced all things to God; compare 2 Samuel 24:1, where the LORD incites David, with 1 Chronicles 21:1, where Satan does. Music's healing power over the troubled mind was noted by ancient writers and is studied today. See the topic on the evil spirit.

echoes: Genesis 25:23; Genesis 37:3; Judges 6:15; Ruth 4:17–22; Psalm 78:70–72; Psalm 89:20; Isaiah 11:1–2; Micah 5:2; Luke 2:4–11; Acts 13:22

settings.what: The LORD sends Samuel to Bethlehem
settings.to: Samuel, still grieving for Saul
settings.when: after Saul's rejection
settings.why: God tells Samuel to stop grieving, fill his horn with oil and go to Jesse, "because I have seen a king for myself among his sons." In chapter 8 the people asked for a king; now God chooses one for himself. God also gives Samuel a cover story of a sacrifice, since Saul would kill him. The anointing is secret, as Saul's was.

settings.to: Samuel, at the sacrifice in Bethlehem
settings.when: when Samuel sees tall Eliab and thinks he must be the one
settings.why: God tells Samuel not to look at Eliab's face or height, because God looks at the heart. Saul was chosen as the tallest man in Israel; David is the youngest, out with the sheep. The words teach readers how God chooses, and they shape how the rest of David's story is read.

traditions.q: The Spirit left Saul. Can a true believer lose salvation?
views: Yes. Mortal sin destroys the grace of justification, though repentance and the sacrament of penance can restore it (Catechism 1855–1861). No one can be sure of persevering to the end without a special revelation (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 12).

Yes. The Augsburg Confession (article 12) rejects the view that those once justified cannot lose the Holy Spirit, so a believer who lives on in sin without repentance can fall away. Yet Lutherans urge believers to trust God's promise rather than doubt it.

No. Those whom God has truly called will persevere to the end, though they may fall into serious sin for a time (Westminster Confession 17). The Spirit's coming on Saul gave him gifts for his office, not saving grace.

Yes. After receiving the Holy Spirit a person may depart from grace and fall into sin, and by God's grace may rise again (Articles of Religion 12; John Wesley, Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints).

No. Genuine believers will never fall away from grace (Baptist Faith and Message, article 5), a teaching many Baptists call eternal security. Saul's story is read as a warning about a man who was never truly changed, or as being about his office as king.

title: David and Goliath
sum: The Philistines camp across the Valley of Elah from Israel. Their champion, Goliath of Gath, a giant in bronze armor, challenges Israel every day for forty days to send one man to fight him. No one goes. David, sent by his father with food for his brothers, hears the challenge and asks who this uncircumcised Philistine is to insult the battle lines of the living God.

David tells Saul that the LORD saved him from lions and bears. He refuses Saul's armor and goes with a stick, a sling and five stones. "You are coming at me with a sword, a spear and a javelin," he says. "I am coming at you in the name of the LORD of Armies." One stone strikes Goliath's forehead. David kills him with his own sword, and the Philistines flee. Then Saul asks: "Whose son is this lad?"
readings: Read as faith against power

The giant has every advantage: size, armor, weapons, experience. David has faith that "the battle belongs to the LORD." The story has become the world's picture of the underdog, but its point is theological: the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear.
Read as two stories in one

The chapter introduces David's family as if for the first time, and Saul does not know David at the end, though David has been his armor-bearer. Many scholars read the long Hebrew text as two accounts combined; others read one carefully built story. See the deep sections below.

views.H: The battle took place in the Valley of Elah, which can still be visited, during Saul's reign. David's victory was real, with a sling against a heavily armed Philistine warrior. Saul's question at the end was about David's family, not his identity.
views.C: Most critical scholars see two versions of how David came to Saul, joined by an editor, and many think the deed was transferred to David from Elhanan (2 Samuel 21:19). The Old Greek text's shorter story is key evidence.
views.L: The story is told with care: Goliath's armor described at length, David's simple tools, speeches that set the theme. The narrator calls Goliath by name only twice; he is "the Philistine," and David is everything Saul is not.
views.J: The rabbis made Goliath a descendant of Orpah, Ruth's sister-in-law, so the battle was between two descendants of Moabite sisters. They praised David's trust in God and his care for God's honor.
views.X: Christian readers have long seen David as a type of Christ, the one who fights alone for his people and wins a victory they share. Others apply the story to the believer's spiritual battles (Ephesians 6:10–17), though some warn against making it a lesson about personal giants.

deep.b:
The oldest Greek text (Codex Vaticanus) lacks about 44 percent of chapters 17–18, 39 of 88 verses by Tov's count, including 17:12–31 and 17:55–18:5. Without them, the story runs smoothly: David, Saul's armor-bearer (16:21), volunteers and wins. The missing passages tell the story of an unknown shepherd boy who comes to the camp with food and, after his victory, is introduced to Saul.

Emanuel Tov and Johan Lust argue that the Greek translates an older, shorter Hebrew text, and that the longer Hebrew adds a second version; the translator of Samuel is usually literal, so he is unlikely to have cut so much. Dominique Barthélemy and D. W. Gooding argue that the long text is a single, artful story, shortened by the Greek translator or his Hebrew source to remove apparent contradictions. Gooding's strongest point is that the short text still has tensions (David is a "lad" untried in war in 17:33 after being called a soldier in 16:18), so the shortening did not make a smooth text, and the long text's repetitions can be design. The four set out their arguments together in The Story of David and Goliath (1986). Since then more scholars have leaned toward Tov and Lust (for example Auld and Ho), but the question is open.

Harmonizing readers (H) point out that 17:15 explains David's coming and going between court and pasture, that Saul's question in 17:55–58 is about David's father ("whose son"), linked to the promised reward (17:25), and that biblical narrative often arranges events by theme. Literary readers (L) note that the doubled introductions serve the story's theme: David is unknown, then known.

2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan of Bethlehem killed "Goliath the Gittite," whose spear was like a weaver's beam. 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan killed "Lahmi the brother of Goliath." There are four main answers. (1) The Chronicles text is right and 2 Samuel 21:19 is a copying error; the letters of "Lahmi" and "the Bethlehemite" are close. (2) Elhanan was David's personal name, and David his throne name (the Targum and Rashi). (3) There were two Goliaths. (4) Elhanan's deed was later credited to the more famous David (many critical scholars, such as Halpern and McCarter). Note that the name "Goliath" appears only twice in this chapter (17:4; 17:23).

The oldest manuscript (4QSam-a), the Old Greek and Josephus say four cubits and a span, about six feet nine inches. The Masoretic Text and Codex Alexandrinus say six cubits and a span, nearly ten feet. The Plain follows "four": three old witnesses agree, and numbers tend to grow in copying, the same reasoning the Plain uses at 13:5. Clyde Billington defends "six," arguing the Greek translators converted the height into royal cubits. See the textual note on 17:4.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the armor tells the story
deep.b: The chapter is built around clothing and weapons. Goliath is described from helmet to spear (17:5–7). Saul puts his own armor on David, and it does not fit (17:38–39). David goes with a shepherd's stick and bag (17:40). He kills Goliath with Goliath's own sword (17:51). Then Jonathan gives David his robe, sword, bow and belt (18:4). The sequence may be a deliberate picture of transfer: the old order's armor fails, the enemy's weapon turns against him, and the heir freely gives what the king could not.

echoes: Numbers 13:33; Joshua 11:22; 2 Samuel 21:15–22; 1 Chronicles 20:4–8; 2 Chronicles 20:15; Psalm 144:1; Ephesians 6:10–17

settings.by: Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath
settings.to: Saul's army, across the Valley of Elah
settings.when: morning and evening for forty days
settings.why: Goliath offers to settle the war by single combat and mocks Israel's army as "Saul's servants." The challenge makes the battle a test of Israel's king, who stands taller than all the people but will not go out. It also leaves room for someone else to fight for Israel.

settings.to: King Saul, in the camp
settings.when: when Saul says he is only a lad
settings.why: David tells how he killed a lion and a bear to save his father's sheep, and says the LORD who saved him from them will save him from the Philistine. He presents himself as a shepherd who protects the flock, which is the old picture of a king. Saul, who should fight, sends David instead.

settings.to: Goliath, and in the hearing of both armies
settings.when: as the two close in for the fight
settings.why: David says he comes "in the name of the LORD of Armies," so that all the earth will know there is a God in Israel. All gathered there will learn that the LORD saves, not by sword and spear. The speech turns a duel into a lesson about God. That is how Israel was meant to hear the story: the battle belongs to the LORD.

title: Loved by All, Hated by Saul
sum: Jonathan's life is tied to David's; he loves him as himself, makes a covenant with him, and gives him his robe and weapons. David succeeds in everything. When the army returns, women sing, "Saul has struck his thousands, David his tens of thousands," and Saul's jealousy begins.

Twice Saul throws a spear at David. He sends him to war, hoping the Philistines will kill him. He offers his daughter Merab, then gives her to another man. When Saul learns his daughter Michal loves David, he sets a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping David will die. David brings two hundred. Everyone loves David; only Saul is his enemy, because the LORD is with David.
readings: Read as the rise of David

The chapter repeats that the LORD was with David (18:12; 18:14; 18:28) and that David acted wisely. Everyone loves him: Jonathan, Michal, all Israel and Judah. This is the language of a story written to show that David's rise was God's will, not a grab for power.
Read as the fall of Saul

Saul moves from love to jealousy to fear to open enmity. Each step is recorded in his own thoughts. He uses his daughters, his army and religious language to destroy David. The narrator lets us inside Saul's mind more than David's.

views.H: David's marriage to Michal and his early military command came a few years into his service at court. The bride-price of foreskins reflects real customs of counting the enemy dead.
views.C: Critical scholars see this chapter as central to the "History of David's Rise," a defense of David's legitimacy. The Old Greek's shorter text lacks Jonathan's covenant, the first spear, and the offer of Merab.
views.L: Robert Alter notes that everyone loves David, but David's own feelings are never stated. Michal is the only woman in Hebrew narrative said to love a man. Saul's inner speech reveals his plans.
views.J: The Mishnah holds up the love of David and Jonathan as the model of love "that does not depend on anything" and so never ends (Avot 5:16).
views.X: Christian readers have often seen Jonathan's self-giving love, handing over his robe and his right to the throne, as a picture of humility and friendship, and David, loved by the people but persecuted by the king, as a type of Christ.

deep.b:
The love between Jonathan and David is read in three main ways, and they are not exclusive.

Covenant loyalty. In ancient treaties "love" was the word for political loyalty, as in the Amarna letters and Deuteronomy 6:5, and J. A. Thompson read Jonathan's love in that light. Jonathan, the heir, makes a covenant (18:3), hands David the robe and weapons of the crown prince (18:4), and later says outright, "You are the one who will reign over Israel, and I will be next to you" (23:17). On this reading the story shows Saul's own heir conceding David's right to the throne. Saul Olyan has shown how much of the vocabulary (love, covenant, loyal love) belongs to this covenant idiom between equals and partners.

Friendship. Jewish and Christian tradition has read a model friendship. The Mishnah calls it the love "that does not depend on anything," and so never ends (Avot 5:16). Kisses and tears between men were normal among kin and friends (Genesis 33:4; Genesis 45:15), and the text uses none of the Bible's sexual vocabulary ("know," "lie with"). Robert Gagnon argues for this reading against the next one.

Romantic or erotic love. Tom Horner and Susan Ackerman read the bond as romantic. They point to Jonathan's "delight" in David (19:1), a verb used of Shechem's desire for Dinah (Genesis 34:19); to Saul's taunt about "the nakedness of your mother" (20:30), using the word of the sexual laws; to the kisses and weeping of 20:41; and to David's lament, "Your love was a wonder to me, / more than the love of women" (2 Samuel 1:26). Ackerman argues that Jonathan is cast in a "liminal," bride-like role toward David.

Most commentators read covenant friendship; a substantial minority sees homoerotic overtones. See the topics on Jonathan and same-sex relations.

echoes: Genesis 44:30; 2 Samuel 1:26; 2 Samuel 3:14; 2 Samuel 11:14–17; Psalm 59; Exodus 15:20–21

settings.to: King Saul and the returning army, with tambourines and dancing
settings.when: as the army comes home after David kills the Philistine
settings.why: The women sing, "Saul has struck his thousands, David his tens of thousands." In Hebrew poetry the two numbers may simply be a pair meaning "many," but Saul hears them as a ranking. The song is quoted again by the Philistines (21:11; 29:5). It sets Saul's jealousy loose and shows that the people already see David as a leader.

settings.to: David
settings.when: when David says he is too poor to marry the king's daughter Michal
settings.why: Saul asks for no bride-price except a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping David will die trying. The narrator tells readers Saul's real aim. David brings two hundred. The plot meant to kill David makes him the king's son-in-law and a step closer to the throne.

title: Escape Through the Window
sum: Saul orders his son and servants to kill David. Jonathan pleads for David, and Saul swears he will not die. But when David wins another battle, the evil spirit seizes Saul, and the spear flies again.

That night, Michal lets David down through a window, puts a household god in his bed, and tells Saul's men he is sick. David flees to Samuel at Ramah. Saul sends three groups of messengers to seize him, and each time the Spirit of God makes them prophesy. Finally Saul goes himself. The Spirit falls on him too, and he lies stripped before Samuel all night. People say, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
readings: Read as protection
Three protectors save David: Jonathan with words, Michal with a trick, and the Spirit of God with power. The king's whole household turns against the king, and even God's Spirit stops his men.
Read as Saul's humiliation
The Spirit that once made Saul a new man (10:6) now leaves him naked and helpless. The proverb first told of his rise (10:11–12) now marks his fall.

views.H: David's escape from his house and to Ramah took place around 1012 BC. Psalm 59, according to its heading, was written about this night.
views.C: Critical scholars see doublets here: the spear scene (18:10–11 and 19:9–10) and the proverb about Saul (10:11–12 and 19:24). They suggest different versions of the same events were preserved.
views.L: The chapter echoes earlier stories: Rahab's window (Joshua 2:15) and Rachel's deceit with household gods (Genesis 31:34–35). Michal, like Rachel, fools her father.
views.J: Jewish tradition held Naioth to be Samuel's school of prophets, a house of study. The rabbis explained Michal's household god as a figure or dummy, not an idol.
views.X: Christian readers have seen the Spirit stopping Saul's men as God's protection of his anointed. Paul's escape through a window in Damascus (Acts 9:25) echoes David's escape.

deep.b: The teraphim were images of household gods or ancestors, sometimes used for divination. Samuel had just condemned them (15:23). How could David's house have one? Some readers think it belonged to Michal. Others note that popular religion in Israel included such objects, and the text simply reports it. Josiah later removed them (2 Kings 23:24). The image must have been human-sized to fool the messengers. See the topic on teraphim.

echoes: 10:5–13; Genesis 31:19–35; Joshua 2:15; Numbers 11:25–29; 2 Kings 1:9–15; Acts 9:25; Psalm 59

settings.to: his father, King Saul, in the field
settings.when: after Saul tells his son and servants to kill David
settings.why: Jonathan reminds Saul that David risked his life against the Philistine and that killing him would be shedding innocent blood. The plea works for a time, and Saul swears David will not die. The king's own heir defends his rival, which helps readers see that David took nothing from Saul's house by force.

title: The Arrows
sum: David flees to Jonathan: what has he done to make Saul want to kill him? Jonathan cannot believe his father would hide such a plan. They agree on a test. David will miss the new moon feast, and Jonathan will learn Saul's reaction. Before the plan, they renew their covenant, and Jonathan asks David to show loyal love to his family forever.

At the feast, David's seat is empty. On the second day Saul explodes, insults Jonathan's mother, and throws a spear at his own son. The next morning Jonathan shoots arrows as the signal. Then the two friends meet, kiss and weep, and part with an oath that binds their families for all time.
readings: Read as covenant

The word "covenant" and "loyal love" (hesed) run through the chapter. Jonathan, the heir, asks the future king for loyalty to his family. The covenant will be kept when David cares for Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9).
Read as friendship

The chapter is one of the most moving portraits of friendship in literature: two men bound by love, in danger, planning by night, and parting in tears. It has been read as a model of loyal friendship ever since.

views.H: The new moon feast was a regular court occasion in Saul's day. David's flight marks the beginning of his years as a fugitive, around 1012 BC.
views.C: Critical scholars see the covenant language (20:14–17; 20:42) as preparing for David's treatment of Saul's family in 2 Samuel 9 and 21, defending David against charges that he wiped out Saul's house.
views.L: The chapter is built around a coded signal: the arrows and the boy who knows nothing. The reader knows what the boy does not. Saul's outburst against Jonathan shows his inner life again.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 20:18–42 as the haftarah when a Sabbath falls on the eve of the new moon (Machar Chodesh). The friendship is the model of love "that does not depend on anything" (Avot 5:16).
views.X: Christian readers see in Jonathan's self-giving loyalty a picture of friendship (John 15:13) and in the covenant with David's house a picture of grace extended to the next generation.

deep.b: Saul calls Jonathan "son of a twisted woman, a rebel" and says he shames "the nakedness of your mother" (20:30). The insult is aimed at Jonathan but falls on Saul's own wife. Some modern readers find a sexual meaning in Saul's accusation that Jonathan has "picked" the son of Jesse; most see a political one, since Saul goes on: as long as David lives, Jonathan's kingship is not secure. Jonathan has chosen David over his own throne.

settings.to: David, alone in the field near Gibeah
settings.when: before the new moon feast, when David fears Saul means to kill him
settings.why: Jonathan swears to tell David the truth about his father's plans. In return he asks that David show the LORD's loyal love to Jonathan's family forever, even when the LORD has cut off all David's enemies. Saul's own son accepts that David will rule. The promise is kept when David cares for Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1–7). For readers, it shows David's kingship sealed by loyalty, not seized.

settings.to: Jonathan, at the king's table
settings.when: on the second day of the new moon feast, when David's seat is empty
settings.why: Saul insults Jonathan and tells him that as long as David lives, Jonathan's kingship will never be secure. In his anger he says aloud what the story wants readers to see. Saul is fighting to keep a throne for his family, and Jonathan has freely given up his claim. Saul then throws a spear at his own son.
